narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7693800) reads this as 'the worldly satisfied with this life', and the type (102, 7693801) files it as an affect — a felt inner state, not an act done. Its locus (116, 7693808) is internal:ib-state and its role (115, 7693810) is characteristic: this is genuinely an interior condition of a human being, not merely an external circumstance. The seat (104, 7693802) is 'none' — the satisfaction is not lodged in a named organ (heart, soul), which fits a contentment that is diffuse and appetitive rather than seated in the deep self. The source (103, present:false) is not recorded: the passage does not say what produces this fullness beyond the circumstance itself. The bearer (105, 7693803) is inferred as 'men of the world', and the operation (106, 7693804) traces the whole movement — men whose portion is in this life are filled with treasure, satisfied with children, and leave their abundance to their infants: a contentment bounded by the present age. The target (107, 7693805) is 'this-life-satisfaction' and the coupling (112, 7693807) is 'worldly-satisfied' — the satisfaction points at, and binds to, only what the present world affords. Manner (108, 7693806) is 'none': no qualifying mode is added; the satisfaction is stated flatly. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) and prohibition (113) are all present:false — the reader recorded no measured degree, no narrowing qualifier, no downstream consequence, and no restriction. The silence on effect is itself telling: a full interior that produces nothing beyond itself, terminating in the infants who inherit the goods. The discovery (114, 7693809) names the finding plainly: the interior of the worldly is filled and content, but only with what this life holds — a satisfaction that stops at the grave. Read against directive 5, this dark or bounded satisfaction is given full weight: it is a real, complete inner fullness, only cut off from anything beyond the present, and the passage sets it deliberately beside the psalmist's own hope in v15 to be satisfied with God's likeness on waking.
narratives.story: This passage looks inside people who have everything the present world can give. Their inner sense of being full and content is real, but it is fastened entirely to what this life holds — money in the treasury, children around the table, an inheritance handed on to the little ones. Scripture does not say where this contentment comes from or where it leads; it simply notes that it settles nowhere deep and produces nothing lasting. It is a fullness with a lid on it, one that stops at the grave. Set beside the writer's own longing to wake and be satisfied with God himself, this satisfied heart is shown to be complete in its own terms yet closed to anything greater.
narratives.variation_note: Of the three readings of 'satisfied' (saba), this is the only one whose bearer is 'men of the world' and whose target/coupling is bounded to 'this life'. Where #2 (Psa 63:5) and #3 (Psa 65:4) read the soul filled BY God, this reads a fullness closed off from God — the same word carrying a descent rather than an ascent, which the passage itself contrasts with v15.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7694496) is 'soul revived by the law', and the type (102, 7694497) is state — a condition the inner being is brought into, not an action it performs. Locus (116, 7694504) is internal:ib-state and role (115, 7694506) is characteristic, so this is a true interior alteration. The seat (104, 7694498) is 'none': though the operation names the soul, the reader recorded no organ-seat for the revival itself, marking it as a whole-self restoration rather than something localised. Source (103, present:false) is not recorded as a discrete row, yet the operation (106, 7694500) supplies the agent implicitly: the perfect law of the LORD revives/restores the soul — the interior brought back to life by the word. The bearer (105, 7694499) is the psalmist. The target (107, 7694501) is 'revival' and the coupling (112, 7694503) is 'soul-revived': the movement runs from the word acting upon, and binding to, the soul that is renewed. Manner (108, 7694502) is 'none' — no mode is specified beyond the plain fact of restoration. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) are all present:false: the reader logged no degree, no qualifier, no consequence beyond the state itself, and no prohibition. The discovery (114, 7694505) crystallises it: the word acts on the soul the way food acts on a faint body — inner restoration as the operation. Per directive 4, the full process is short but complete: an external, perfect word touches the interior and the faint self is brought back to life; the passage locates the whole cluster of v7-9 benefits (wisdom, joy, light) around this first act of reviving.
narratives.story: Here a tired, drooping inner life is brought back to life by God's word. Scripture compares it to what food does for someone who has fainted — the law of the Lord reaches the soul and revives it. It is not something the person achieves; it is a state they are restored into, touching the whole self rather than one corner of it. The writer does not spell out degrees or after-effects; the point is simply the coming-back-to-life. The perfect word arrives from outside and the weary interior is quickened.

narratives.narrative: This reading is an absence read as evidence (directive 2). The sense (101, 7695100) is 'none to help' and the type (102, 7695101) is state — the inner condition here is the felt state of having no helper, not an act of helping. Locus (116, 7695108) is internal:ib-state, role (115, 7695110) characteristic: the helplessness is treated as a real interior condition of the psalmist. Seat (104, 7695102) is 'none' — no organ houses this; it is the whole self's exposure. Source (103, present:false) is unrecorded. The bearer (105, 7695103) is the psalmist, and the operation (106, 7695104) traces the movement: the self pleads that God not be far, for trouble is near and there is none to help — utter isolation. The target (107, 7695105) is 'helplessness' and the coupling (112, 7695107) is 'none-to-help': the whole inner movement points at, and binds to, the emptiness where a helper should be. Manner (108, 7695106) is 'none'. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all present:false — no degree, qualifier, consequence, or restriction is logged; the bareness of the record matches the bareness the verse describes. The discovery (114, 7695109) reads it: the operation names the aloneness — every human support has failed, leaving only God to appeal to. Under directive 5 this is a genuinely dark interior state and is read at full weight: 'help' appears here only in its negation, and that negation is the finding — the inner being stripped of every prop, its plea for nearness rising precisely because no one is left to help.
narratives.story: This is the inner experience of having no one. Trouble is closing in, and the writer's cry is that God would not stay far away, because there is no one at all to help. The word 'help' appears here only as something absent — every human support has fallen away. It is not an action but a state: the bare, exposed feeling of being utterly alone. And it is out of that emptiness, with only God left to appeal to, that the plea for nearness rises.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7695478) is 'your rod and staff comfort me', and the type (102, 7695479) is affect — a felt consolation. Locus (116, 7695486) is internal:ib-state, role (115, 7695488) characteristic: a genuine inner state. Seat (104, 7695480) is 'none' — the comfort is not organ-located but pervades the self as it passes through the valley. Source (103, present:false) is not a separate row, yet the operation (106, 7695482) makes the agent plain: the shepherd's rod and staff comfort the self — a felt consolation from God's guiding, protecting nearness. The bearer (105, 7695481) is the psalmist. The target (107, 7695483) is 'consolation' and the coupling (112, 7695485) is 'comforted': the movement runs from the instruments of the shepherd, through the self, to the state of being consoled. Manner (108, 7695484) is 'none' — no mode is added beyond the bare consolation. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) are present:false: no measured degree, qualifier, downstream effect, or restriction is recorded. The discovery (114, 7695487) sharpens the finding: the very instruments of guidance and defence — the rod and staff — become a source of comfort; the interior is soothed by what also disciplines and protects. Per directive 4 the process is complete though compact: God's near, guarding presence, felt through its tools, produces consolation in a self walking through the shadow of death — fear displaced not by the removal of danger but by accompaniment ('for you are with me').
narratives.story: Walking through the darkest valley, the writer finds his inner fear replaced by comfort. What comforts him is the shepherd's rod and staff — the very tools used to guide and to guard. God's protecting nearness, felt through those instruments, soothes him. The danger is not removed; rather, he is consoled because he is not alone in it. It is a settled inner ease that comes simply from the presence of one who guides and defends.
narratives.variation_note: Of the three readings of 'comforted' (nacham), this one is comfort RECEIVED and felt, sourced in God's guiding nearness (rod and staff). It differs from #2 (Psa 77:2), where the same comfort is REFUSED by the soul, and from #3 (Psa 86:17), where comfort is God's answer to a lament and is paired with being helped. Here consolation is present and accepted mid-danger.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7652488) is 'renew / make new (chadash — a right spirit)', and the type (102, 7652489) is action — unlike the state-readings elsewhere in this family, renewal here is an act (petitioned of God). Locus (116, 7652496) is internal:spirit — notably not the generic internal:ib-state, but specifically the spirit — and role (115, 7652498) is characteristic. The seat (104, 7652490) is recorded as a span-resolved pair 'within me (the spirit)' (from_span 279648 to_span 279650): the renewal is precisely seated within, in the spirit, making this the most explicitly located reading in the family. Source (103, present:false) is not a separate row, but the address 'O God' makes God the implied agent of the making-new. The bearer (105, 7652491) is 'the penitent'. The operation (106, 7652492) is 'be renewed'. The target (107, 7652493) is a span-pair 'a right / steadfast spirit' (279648 to 279650): the inner disposition is what is remade. Manner (108, 7652494) is 'within me' — an interior mode, reinforcing that this happens inside the self, not at the surface. The coupling (112, 7652495) is a span-pair 'paired with the created clean heart' (279648 to 279645): renewal (chadash) is twinned with creation (bara) of the clean heart — two verbs for one interior re-founding. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) are present:false: no degree, qualifier, consequence, or restriction logged. The discovery (114, 7652497) reads the whole: the inner disposition made new and firm; a steadfast spirit set right within, the will re-established toward God after collapse. Per directives 4 and 8 the process is a re-founding after moral ruin — the penitent asks God to remake the interior itself, the spirit made steadfast, distinct from yet paired with the clean-heart creation, so that the difference between renewing and creating is preserved as two facets of one restoration.
narratives.story: After his sin, the writer asks God to make his inner life new again — to set a steadfast spirit right inside him. This is not a feeling that comes over him but something he begs God to do: to rebuild the will and disposition that had collapsed. It happens deep within, in the spirit, and it stands alongside his other plea, that God would create in him a clean heart. Two pictures — making new and creating fresh — describe one act of inner re-founding. The self that had broken down is to be re-established, firm and turned back toward God.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7656467) is 'be satisfied / filled (saba — my soul will be satisfied as with fat)', and the type (102, 7656468) is status — a settled condition. Locus (116, 7656475) is internal:ib-state, role (115, 7656477) characteristic. Uniquely among the satisfaction-readings, the seat (104, 7656469) is a span-pair 'the soul' (from_span 281062 to_span 281061): this satisfaction is seated in the nephesh, the deep self that in v1 thirsted and fainted. The bearer (105, 7656470) is also a span-pair 'the psalmist (his soul)' (281062 to 281061) — bearer and seat converge on the soul. Source (103, present:false) is unrecorded as a row, but the surrounding verses make God the one who fills. The operation (106, 7656471) is 'be satisfied / filled' (inferred, to_span 281062). The target (107, 7656472) is 'none' — strikingly, no object is named: the soul is simply filled, and the absence of a target says the fullness is not fixed on a thing but is a state of the self. Manner (108, 7656473) is 'as with fat and rich food' — the mode is banquet-richness, answering the desert of v1. The coupling (112, 7656474) is a span-pair 'issues in joyful praise' (281062 to 281066): the satisfaction does not terminate in itself but overflows into praise with joyful lips. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7656476) reads the arc: the thirst of v1 answered with the fullness of a feast — desert-longing turned to banquet-satisfaction, the richest fare found in God himself. Per directive 4 the full movement runs from a fainting, thirsting soul in a dry land to a soul sated as at a feast, and onward into joyful praise — an ascent whose coupling to praise is the distinguishing note.
narratives.story: The writer began this psalm thirsting for God like a man in a waterless desert. Now he says his inner self will be satisfied as if seated at a rich feast. The deep longing of the soul is answered, not by any particular thing, but by being filled to fullness in God himself. And that fullness does not stop there — it spills over into joyful praise on his lips. The dry, fainting self of the opening has become a soul richly fed and singing.
narratives.variation_note: Among the three 'satisfied' readings this is the individual soul (nephesh) filled BY God after desert-thirst, seated in the soul and overflowing into praise. It differs from #1 (Psa 17:14), a worldly fullness bounded to this life, and from #3 (Psa 65:4), a corporate 'we' satisfied with the goodness of God's house — here the bearer is one longing soul and the coupling is to joyful praise.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7657069) is 'be satisfied / filled (saba — we shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house)', and the type (102, 7657070) is status. Locus (116, 7657077) is internal:ib-state, role (115, 7657079) characteristic. The seat (104, 7657071) is 'none' — unlike #2 (seated in the soul), here no organ is named: the fullness is corporate and diffuse across the worshippers rather than lodged in one deep self. The bearer (105, 7657072) is inferred as 'the worshippers' — a plural 'we', not a single psalmist. Source (103, present:false) is unrecorded as a row, but the passage's flow (chosen, brought near, dwelling in the courts) makes God the fount. The operation (106, 7657073) is 'be satisfied / filled'. The target (107, 7657074) is a span-pair 'with the goodness of God's house' (281207 to 281208), and the manner (108, 7657075) is a span-pair 'with the holiness of his temple' (281207 to 281210): the fullness is qualified twice — its object is the house's goodness, its mode the temple's holiness. The coupling (112, 7657076) is a span-pair 'the fullness that flows from being brought near' (281207 to 281202): satisfaction is bound to the prior act of being chosen and brought near to dwell in the courts. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7657078) reads it: the soul filled by God's own goodness — the deep contentment of those near God, the fullness of communion, as in Ps 63:5. Per directives 4 and 8 the process runs from being chosen and drawn near, to dwelling in the courts, to a satisfaction whose very content is God's goodness and holiness; the corporate bearer and the explicit target/manner distinguish it from the individual soul of #2.
narratives.story: This is the contentment of people God has chosen and brought near to live in his presence. Together they say they will be filled and satisfied — not with ordinary things, but with the goodness of God's house and the holiness of his temple. The fullness flows directly out of being drawn close to him. It is not one lonely soul being fed here but a whole company of worshippers, satisfied by God's own goodness. Nearness to God is itself the feast.
narratives.variation_note: This 'satisfied' reading has a corporate bearer ('the worshippers', a 'we') and no seat, with the fullness explicitly qualified by the house's goodness and the temple's holiness and coupled to being brought near. It differs from #2 (Psa 63:5), an individual soul seated in the nephesh overflowing into praise, and from #1 (Psa 17:14), a worldly fullness closed to God. Same word, communion-satisfaction shared among many.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7660220) is 'revive / live (chayah — let your hearts revive)', and the type (102, 7660221) is status — a condition the seekers are summoned into. Locus (116, 7660228) is internal:heart and role (115, 7660230) characteristic. The seat (104, 7660222) is a span-pair 'the heart' (from_span 281845 to_span 281844): the reviving is explicitly heart-seated, distinct from the soul-revival of Psa 19:7. Source (103, present:false) is not a separate row, yet the context — the LORD who hears the needy (v33) — supplies the implied ground. The bearer (105, 7660223) is inferred as 'those who seek God'. The operation (106, 7660224) is 'revive / come alive' (inferred, to_span 281845). The target (107, 7660225) is 'none' — no object beyond the coming-alive itself; the absence marks revival as an intransitive quickening of the self. Manner (108, 7660226) is a span-pair 'in the heart' (281845 to 281844) — the mode is interior, in the heart. The coupling (112, 7660227) is a span-pair 'the reviving of the seekers' hearts' (281845 to 281841): the reviving is bound to the seeing of God's help ('when the humble see it they will be glad'). Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7660229) reads it: the heart brought back to life — drooping faith quickened again by God's care for the needy, the fainting made to live. Per directive 4 the movement runs from humble seekers watching God act for the needy, to their fainting hearts coming alive again; it is a corporate imperative-invitation ('let your hearts revive') rather than a personal restoration.
narratives.story: To people who seek God but whose courage has drooped, the psalm says: let your hearts come alive again. Watching God act on behalf of the needy and afflicted, their fainting inner life is quickened once more. It is centred in the heart — a coming-back-to-life with no object beyond the reviving itself. This is not one person's private restoration but an invitation to a whole company of seekers. Seeing that God cares for the lowly, their hearts revive.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7661358) is 'give deliverance / save (yasha — give deliverance to the children of the needy)', and the type (102, 7661359) is action — a deed done, not a state undergone. Crucially the locus (116, 7661366) is external:person, not the internal loci that dominate this family: this is an inner-being characteristic (role 115, 7661368, characteristic) that expresses itself as outward saving action toward another. The seat (104, 7661360) is 'none' — no organ; consistent with an outward act. Source (103, present:false) is unrecorded. The bearer (105, 7661361) is 'the king': the interior disposition analysed here is the king's, made visible in what he does. The operation (106, 7661362) is 'give deliverance / save'. The target (107, 7661363) is a span-pair 'the children of the needy' (282317 to 282319) — the most vulnerable are the object. Manner (108, 7661364) is 'none'. The coupling (112, 7661365) is a span-pair 'paired with defending the poor and crushing the oppressor' (282317 to 282320): deliverance is bound into a triad — defend the poor, deliver the needy's children, crush the oppressor. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7661367) reads it: the king rescuing the helpless — deliverance extended to the most vulnerable, the king a savior to the poor. Per directives 3 and 4 the inner-being lens holds even though the locus is external: the king's saving character is the process — an interior orientation toward the helpless that issues in defending, delivering, and crushing what oppresses them.
narratives.story: This describes the heart of the ideal king, shown in what he does. His inner bent toward the helpless comes out as action: he defends the poor, rescues the children of the needy, and crushes those who oppress them. The saving reaches all the way down to the most vulnerable — the little ones of the poorest. It is not a private feeling but a character that acts, turning royal power into protection for those who cannot protect themselves. The king becomes a rescuer of the weak.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7661424) is 'save (yasha — the lives of the needy he saves)', and the type (102, 7661425) is action. Locus (116, 7661432) is external:person and role (115, 7661434) characteristic: the king's inner compassion expressed as an outward act. Seat (104, 7661426) is 'none'. Source (103, present:false) unrecorded. The bearer (105, 7661427) is 'the king'. The operation (106, 7661428) is 'save'. The target (107, 7661429) is a span-pair 'the lives of the needy' (282248 to 282249) — the very lives, not merely the circumstances, of the poor. Manner (108, 7661430) is 'none'. The coupling (112, 7661431) is a span-pair 'the act that flows from his pity' (282248 to 282244): saving is bound directly to the prior 'he has pity on the weak and the needy' — the deed springs from an inner movement of compassion. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7661433) reads it: the king's compassion made rescue — pity turned into deliverance, mercy that acts. Per directives 4 and 8 the finding is precisely the linkage preserved in the coupling: pity is the interior source, saving the outward operation, the needy's lives the target — the difference from the neighbouring 'redeems' and 'delivers' lies in this reading's stress on pity issuing in the saving of life itself.
narratives.story: Here the king's inner pity turns into action: he saves the lives of the needy. What moves him is compassion for the weak and poor, and that compassion does not stay a feeling — it becomes rescue. It reaches their very lives, not just their comfort. The mercy inside him is a mercy that acts. Pity becomes deliverance.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7661435) is 'redeem (gaal — from oppression and violence he redeems their life)', and the type (102, 7661436) is action. Locus (116, 7661443) is external:person, role (115, 7661445) characteristic: again the king's interior mercy shown in deed. Seat (104, 7661437) is 'none'. Source (103, present:false) unrecorded. The bearer (105, 7661438) is 'the king'. The operation (106, 7661439) is 'redeem' — and the verb is weighty: gaal is the kinsman-redeemer's act, buying back what is enslaved or forfeited. The target (107, 7661440) is a span-pair 'their life, from oppression and violence' (282255 to 282256). Manner (108, 7661441) is inferred 'their blood precious in his sight' — the mode is a valuing: he redeems because he holds their very blood precious. The coupling (112, 7661442) is a span-pair 'the climax of the king's saving compassion' (282255 to 282248): redeeming crowns the sequence pity-save-redeem, bound to the saving of v13. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7661444) reads it: the king ransoming the oppressed, valuing their very lives — the redeeming (a kinsman's act) of the poor from cruelty, the highest reach of royal mercy. Per directives 8 and 10 the distinction is preserved: where 'saves' stressed pity-into-rescue and 'delivers' the answer to a cry, 'redeems' adds the kinsman-ransom note and the valuing of the lowly's blood — the deepest, most costly form of the king's saving character.
narratives.story: This is the king's mercy at its highest reach: he ransoms the lives of the oppressed out of cruelty and violence, like a kinsman buying back his own. He does it because he holds their very blood precious — the lives of the lowly matter to him. It is the peak of a rising sequence: he pities them, he saves them, and now he redeems them at cost. The poorest are treated as worth rescuing at any price. Their lives are precious in his sight.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7661402) is 'deliver (natsal — he delivers the needy who calls)', and the type (102, 7661403) is action. Locus (116, 7661410) is external:person, role (115, 7661412) characteristic: the king's inner readiness shown in deed. Seat (104, 7661404) is 'none'. Source (103, present:false) unrecorded. The bearer (105, 7661405) is 'the king'. The operation (106, 7661406) is 'deliver'. The target (107, 7661407) is a span-pair 'the needy who calls, the poor with no helper' (306652 to 306653) — the object is defined by helplessness and by a cry. Manner (108, 7661408) is inferred 'answering the cry of the helpless': the mode is responsiveness, deliverance triggered by a call. The coupling (112, 7661409) is a span-pair 'paired with pity and saving the weak (v13)' (306652 to 282244): delivering is bound to the same pity-cluster as saves and redeems. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7661411) reads it: the king responsive to the cry of the destitute — the rescue extended to the one with no other help, the ideal king as the last resort of the helpless, mirroring God himself. Per directive 10 the distinguishing note against 'saves' and 'redeems' is responsiveness-to-a-cry: this reading foregrounds the call ('when he calls') and the absence of any other helper, so the king's character is defined as the last resort of those with no one else — the same helplessness named in Psa 22:11, here met by a deliverer.
narratives.story: This shows the king as the one who answers when the helpless call. The needy cry out, the poor have no one else to turn to, and he delivers them. What marks this out is the responsiveness: his rescue is set off by their cry, and it reaches exactly those who have no other helper. He becomes the last resort of people with nowhere else to go. In this the king mirrors God himself, who does not ignore the cry of the destitute.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7663423) is 'be comforted (nacham — to be comforted)', and the type (102, 7663424) is state. Locus (116, 7663431) is internal:ib-state, role (115, 7663433) characteristic. The seat (104, 7663425) is a span-pair 'the soul (nephesh)' (282951 to 282949): the comfort here is soul-seated — and it is refused. The bearer (105, 7663426) is the psalmist. The operation (106, 7663427) is 'be comforted (refused)', recorded as a span-pair (282951 to 282950) — the operation itself carries the negation: the comforting is declined by the very soul that could receive it. The target (107, 7663428) is 'none'. Manner (108, 7663429) is inferred 'withheld / declined': the mode is refusal. The coupling (112, 7663430) is a span-pair 'the comfort the soul refuses' (282951 to 282950): comfort and its refusal are bound in one movement. Source (103), intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7663432) reads it: the consolation the soul will not accept — comfort named only to be declined, the shape of unassuageable grief. Per directives 5 and 6 this uncomfortable, dark reading is given full weight: comfort appears here as something actively refused by the interior, not merely absent. The soul, remembering God, moans and its spirit faints (v3); the very self that might be consoled turns consolation away — a genuine, self-chosen closure against relief that is as much a part of the inner life as its acceptance elsewhere.
narratives.story: This is grief that will not be comforted. In his trouble the writer reaches out to God through the night, yet his very soul refuses to be comforted. Comfort is named here only to be turned away — the inner self shutting the door on relief. Remembering God brings not solace but moaning, and his spirit grows faint. It is the raw shape of a sorrow that, for now, refuses every consolation offered to it.
narratives.variation_note: This 'comforted' reading is the dark one: comfort is soul-seated but REFUSED — the operation itself is 'be comforted (refused)', the manner 'withheld/declined'. It stands against #1 (Psa 23:4), where comfort is received through God's nearness, and #3 (Psa 86:17), where comfort is God's granted answer to lament. The same word here marks a self actively closing against relief.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7664109) is 'be filled / sated (saba)', and the type (102, 7664110) is state. Locus (116, 7664117) is internal:ib-state, role (115, 7664119) characteristic. Seat (104, 7664111) is 'none' — the fullness is appetitive, not organ-seated. Source (103, present:false) is unrecorded as a row, but the operation makes clear God is the giver. The bearer (105, 7664112) is 'they' — the wilderness generation. The operation (106, 7664113) is 'be sated'. The target (107, 7664114) is inferred 'with the craved food'. Manner (108, 7664115) is 'none'. The coupling (112, 7664116) is inferred 'paired with the craving God indulged': the sating is bound to the craving that preceded it — God gave them what they craved. Per directives 5 and 6 this reading is dark and must not be softened: the fullness here is real and complete ('they ate and were well filled'), yet it sits inside a narrative of judgement — before they had done with their craving, while the food was still in their mouths, God's anger rose against them (v30-31). The satiety is genuine but ruinous: an inner fullness granted as the very instrument of judgement, the answered appetite becoming a snare. This stands in deliberate contrast to the soul filled by God's goodness (Psa 63:5, 65:4) — here the same saba is a craving indulged unto death.
narratives.story: In the wilderness, God gave the people exactly what they craved, and they ate and were well filled. The fullness was real — appetite satisfied to the brim. But it came inside a story of judgement: while the food was still in their mouths, God's anger rose against them. Their satisfied craving became the very means of their ruin. This is a fullness that is complete and yet deadly — an indulged appetite that leads not to life but to disaster, the dark shadow of a soul truly satisfied by God.

Seat (104, 7665848) is 'none' — no organ named. Source (103, present:false) unrecorded as a row, yet the speaker is God ('I would satisfy you'), so God is the implied giver. The bearer (105, 7665849) is inferred 'you (Israel)'. The operation (106, 7665850) is 'be satisfied'. The target (107, 7665851) is inferred 'by God' — the fullness would come from God himself. Manner (108, 7665852) is 'none'. The coupling (112, 7665853) is inferred 'paired with the finest wheat and honey': the satisfying is bound to the imagery of finest wheat and honey from the rock. The discovery (114, 7665855) reads it: the full contentment God would give the obedient, blessing withheld only by their refusal. Per directives 4 and 6 the process here is conditional and unrealised: the whole clause is contrary-to-fact ('I WOULD satisfy you'), so this is a satisfaction offered but not received — its non-occurrence is the finding. God stands ready to fill Israel with the richest fare, and the only barrier is the people's own refusal to listen (the psalm's complaint). The reading thus holds a real, God-sourced fullness in suspension: available, generous, and forfeited.
narratives.story: God speaks here of the fullness he longs to give: he would feed his people with the finest wheat and satisfy them with honey from the rock. It is the richest contentment imaginable, and it would come straight from him. But the whole promise hangs on a word — 'would'. It is an offer left unfulfilled, held back not by any lack in God but by the people's refusal to listen to him. The feast is spread and ready; only their own turning away keeps them from it.

Seat (104, 7667337) is 'none' — not organ-located, a whole-self consolation. Source (103, present:false) unrecorded as a row, but the address makes God the comforter ('you, LORD, have... comforted me'). The bearer (105, 7667338) is the psalmist. The operation (106, 7667339) is 'be comforted'. The target (107, 7667340) is inferred 'by God'. Manner (108, 7667341) is 'none'. The coupling (112, 7667342) is inferred 'paired with being helped': comfort is bound to help — 'you have helped me and comforted me' — the two acts joined as one answer to the lament. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7667344) reads it: the consolation God gives, the answered lament turned to comfort. Per directives 4 and 10 the process runs from a besieged self (insolent and ruthless men rising against him, v14) crying for a sign of favour, to God's answer experienced as both help and comfort — and the distinguishing note against the other two 'comforted' readings is exactly this granted, God-given consolation joined to help. Where Psa 77:2 refused comfort and Psa 23:4 felt it in the shepherd's nearness, here comfort is the concrete outcome of an answered prayer, publicly visible so that those who hate him see and are shamed.
narratives.story: Surrounded by insolent, ruthless enemies, the writer asks God for a sign of his favour — and finds himself both helped and comforted. The consolation comes as God's direct answer to his cry; the two go together, help and comfort as one act of rescue. It is not a feeling he works up but something God gives, settling his troubled inner self. And it is meant to be seen: his enemies will watch and be put to shame because the Lord has stood by him. The lament ends in comfort granted.
narratives.variation_note: This 'comforted' reading is comfort GRANTED by God as the answer to a lament, paired with being helped and publicly vindicating. It differs from #1 (Psa 23:4), comfort felt through the shepherd's nearness mid-danger, and from #2 (Psa 77:2), comfort refused by the grieving soul. Here the same word names an answered prayer turned to consolation.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7667646) is 'full (saba)', and the type (102, 7667647) is state. Locus (116, 7667654) is internal:ib-state, role (115, 7667656) characteristic. Seat (104, 7667648) is 'none'. Source (103, present:false) unrecorded. The bearer (105, 7667649) is the psalmist. The operation (106, 7667650) is 'be sated / glutted' — the same fullness-verb (saba) used elsewhere for satisfaction, here turned to its opposite content. The target (107, 7667651) is inferred 'with troubles': the self is filled, but with grief. Manner (108, 7667652) is 'none'. The coupling (112, 7667653) is inferred 'paired with the soul and troubles': the satiety is bound to the soul and its afflictions, the life drawing near to Sheol. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7667655) reads it: satiety of suffering, filled to the brim with grief. Per directives 5 and 6 this is the starkest inversion in the family and is read at full weight: the vocabulary of fullness — the very word for a soul satisfied with God's goodness (Psa 63:5, 65:4) — is here bent to describe a soul glutted with troubles. The inner being is not empty but overfull, saturated with affliction to the point that life itself draws near to the grave. Fullness, ordinarily the mark of blessing, becomes the measure of despair: the self can hold no more suffering.
narratives.story: The writer uses the language of being full — but full of the wrong thing. His inner self is not satisfied with good; it is glutted with troubles, saturated with grief until his very life is sliding toward the grave. The same word that elsewhere describes a soul richly fed by God is here bent to its opposite: a self so crammed with suffering it can hold no more. This is fullness as despair. His trouble has filled him to the brim.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101, 7681354) is 'comfort (nechamah)' — the noun, the thing itself, distinct from the verb nacham read elsewhere in this family. The type (102, 7681355) is state. Locus (116, 7681362) is internal:ib-state, role (115, 7681364) characteristic. Seat (104, 7681356) is 'none'. Source (103, present:false) is not a separate row, but the verse names the ground plainly: God's promise. The bearer (105, 7681357) is the psalmist. The operation (106, 7681358) is 'be comforted'. The target (107, 7681359) is 'none'. Manner (108, 7681360) is 'none'. The coupling (112, 7681361) is inferred 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm': the comfort is bound into the psalm's larger movement of clinging to the word. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7681363) reads it: the consolation the promise brings in affliction — 'This is my comfort in my affliction, that your promise gives me life.' Per directive 4 the process runs from affliction, through God's promise, to a comfort that is specifically life-giving: the word does not merely soothe but revives ('your promise gives me life'), tying this consolation to the reviving/life strand of the family. The comfort is located in the interior yet grounded wholly outside the self, in the reliability of God's spoken promise — an anchor held in the midst of derision (v51) and affliction.
narratives.story: In the middle of his affliction, the writer names what holds him up: his comfort is that God's promise gives him life. The consolation is real and inward, but it rests entirely on something outside himself — the trustworthy word of God. It is not a vague soothing; the promise actually revives him, breathing life into an afflicted heart. Mocked and pressed on every side, he finds his steadiness in what God has said. The word is his comfort.

Notably the locus (116, 7683688) is external:god: the cry is directed outward, toward God, unlike the internal-state loci of most of the family. Role (115, 7683690) is characteristic. The target (107, 7683685) is inferred 'God's word' — the cry is bound to hope in the word ('I hope in your words'). Manner (108, 7683686) is 'none'. The coupling (112, 7683687) is inferred 'paired within its char-arc across the psalm'. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) present:false. The discovery (114, 7683689) reads it: the pre-dawn cry, hoping in the word — 'I rise before dawn and cry for help; I hope in your words.' Per directives 3 and 4 the inner-being process is the outward-directed act of appeal: an interior hope (in God's word) drives a self out of sleep before daybreak to cry for help. This stands in pointed contrast to Psa 22:11, where 'help' was the felt absence of any helper; here the same theme becomes active, hopeful petition — the self not sinking in helplessness but rising early to call on God, its cry grounded in expectant hope in his promises.
narratives.story: Before the sun is up, the writer is already awake and crying out to God for help. This 'help' is not something he passively receives but something he actively reaches for — an urgent appeal driven by hope. What underwrites the cry is his confidence in God's word; he calls out because he trusts what God has promised. Where elsewhere a sufferer feels utterly without a helper, here the same longing becomes early-morning prayer full of expectation. He rises in the dark and cries out, hoping in God's words.
